The musical explores the destructive force of possession, jealousy, and unequal power over a woman determined to remain free. It also sets Carmen’s self-sacrifice against José’s divided loyalties, showing how desire and fear can turn a community’s public spectacle into tragedy.

show: Metro, the Polish musical with music by Janusz Stokłosa, book and lyrics by Agata and Maryna Miklaszewska, directed by Janusz Józefowicz at Teatr Studio Buffo
synopsis:
Jan brings a restless band of young singers, dancers, and street performers into the underground world of the metro, where the platforms become both their refuge and their stage. For Jan, the tunnels are home and the underground is a way of life; for the others, they are a place to carry private histories, ambitions, disappointments, and hopes that have found no welcome elsewhere. Among them is Anka, whose longing for a different life draws her into Jan’s orbit. Their connection grows amid the noise, motion, and improvised community beneath the city.

Above ground, the young performers submit themselves to a theatre audition led by Filip, hoping that professional recognition will turn their dreams into careers. The audition exposes their vulnerability as much as their talent, and the group is rejected. Rather than disperse, they transform their failure into an act of defiance: on the metro platforms, they create their own musical for passing passengers. What begins as an illicit, makeshift performance gathers energy and attention. Their underground show becomes a sensation, allowing the performers to experience the exhilaration of being seen on their own terms.

Success also brings a more dangerous temptation. The commercial theatre that dismissed them now offers the young artists paid work and the prospect of fame. The offer divides the group, forcing each person to weigh security, money, and public success against artistic independence, loyalty, and the ideals that drove them underground in the first place. Jan resists the system that wants to absorb their work, while Anka is caught between the promise of a future and the emotional bond that has formed between them. Love, betrayal, and competing desires test the fragile solidarity of the company as they decide what their dreams are worth.

The show centres on the tension between freedom and commercial success, and on the price of turning art into a career. It also treats youthful idealism, romantic love, and collective creativity as forces strong enough to challenge rejection and disappointment.

show: POLITA, the Polish musical about Pola Negri by Janusz Józefowicz and Janusz Stokłosa at Teatr Studio Buffo in Warsaw
synopsis:
A young Apolonia Chałupiec watches her father taken away from Warsaw’s Powiśle, his exile to Siberia leaving the family in poverty and the child determined to escape its limits. As she grows into Pola Negri, training and early success carry her from Warsaw to Berlin, where Ernst Lubitsch recognises her force on screen and becomes a demanding protector in the absence of her father. Their work propels Pola toward the new world of Paramount and Hollywood, where she turns herself into an international idol.

In America, Pola moves through studios, premieres and the glitter of the Ziegfeld revue. Fame brings romance as well as spectacle: she encounters Charlie Chaplin and dances with Rudolf Valentino, whose intimacy and charisma deepen the intensity of her public life. Yet the height of her success proves unstable. Valentino’s death shatters Pola, and the 1929 crash on Wall Street turns glamour into financial and emotional precarity. The arrival of sound film further disrupts the persona that silent cinema had made irresistible.

Seeking a way back, Pola returns to Europe and confronts Berlin as it darkens under Nazism. Her connection to Ernst Lubitsch and her position in the German film world place her in conflict with Joseph Goebbels; despite restrictions, intervention from Hitler enables her to continue working. The accommodation becomes a lasting burden. As war closes in, Pola leaves through Paris and Portugal for the United States, but Hollywood no longer welcomes her as before. Her former association with Germany, compounded by the changing industry and her Polish accent, leaves her isolated while Gloria Swanson rises as the new symbol of screen success. Pola’s journey ends not in the triumph she imagined, but in the shadow of a legend she can no longer reclaim.

The musical frames ambition as both a source of liberation and a force that demands a personal price. It examines fame’s fragility, the collision of private love with public myth, and the way political catastrophe can permanently reshape an artist’s identity.

show: Musical 1989, the Polish rap musical with music by Andrzej Webber Mikosz and book and lyrics by Marcin Napiórkowski
synopsis:
Lechu scales the gate of Stocznia Gdańska as a workers’ protest gathers force, and the private lives of three couples become entangled with a country’s struggle to change its future. Alongside Danusia, Lechu is pulled from the demands of home and family into public leadership; Władek and Krysia Frasyniuk confront the risks that political commitment brings to a marriage and a household; Jacek and Gaja Kuroń face the same collision of conviction, responsibility, fear, and love. Around them, BOGDAN, ALINA, HENRYKA, ANNA, ZOFIA and other organisers, workers, and allies turn scattered anger into collective action.

The strikes lead to the August agreements and the rise of Solidarność, but the surge of hope is followed by repression. GENERAŁ imposes martial law; arrests, internment, prison cells, surveillance, and separation test not only the resolve of the opposition but also the people waiting at home. The women do not remain on the margins of the political story: Danusia shoulders the public burden of Lechu’s absence and accepts the Nobel Peace Prize in his place, while Krysia, Gaja, and the other women absorb the emotional and practical cost of resistance. Their relationships survive through arguments, exhausted tenderness, humour, and the refusal to abandon one another.

As the decade advances, clandestine resistance and daily endurance give way to negotiation. Lechu, Władek, JACEK, and their allies enter talks in Magdalenka and then the Okrągły Stół, confronting representatives of the ruling order, including MINISTER. The prospect of compromise divides loyalties and raises a painful question: whether a negotiated victory can honour those who endured the struggle. The partially free elections of 1989 bring a decisive opening, transforming an unlikely alliance of workers, dissidents, families, and friends into a force capable of remaking public life.

The show’s central themes are solidarity as a lived commitment, the human price of political courage, and the crucial labour of women within collective change. It also asks how hope, compromise, and imperfect victories can create a shared future without erasing personal sacrifice.

show: Serce ze szkła. Musical zen, the Polish experimental musical with libretto by Klaudia Hartung-Wójciak and Maria Peszek, directed by Cezary Tomaszewski at STUDIO teatrgaleria
synopsis:
Kaj is carried into a wintry, unruly world where an intimate question—whether Jan can truly love after surviving a heart attack—opens a searching passage through family memory, desire, illness, faith, and theatrical fable. Maria and Jan Peszek move through the story beside shifting incarnations of Gerda: Maryjka, Ren, Mania, Maryśka, and others who take up the task of finding, confronting, and refusing to abandon Kaj. Their route crosses the frozen nights of the “zima stulecia,” distant marshes, deserted churches, episodes of ecstasy, and places where loneliness, creative exhaustion, bodily embarrassment, and death are allowed to appear without decorum.

The journey is populated by Królowa Śniegu—both her commanding presence and Królowa Śniegu W Kryzysie—along with Wrona, Kruk, Gołębica, Finka, Matka Kaja, Lapończyk, Zbójniczka, and the unsettling figures of Specjalistka Od Andersena and Dejmek. Kaj’s separation and the Gerdas’ pursuit do not resolve into a simple contest of virtue and evil. Instead, encounters with the castle of Zbójniczka, osiedle Teofilów, church-going companions, birds, strangers, and dancers keep breaking the story open, pulling its characters between tenderness and rage, sacred language and profanity, comic release and emotional crisis.

As Maria and Jan’s relationship comes increasingly to the foreground, the adventure becomes an anatomy of a fragile heart: a father and daughter test inherited expectations of the “good family,” challenge the answers already prepared for them, and continue toward one another despite not knowing how love should look. The ending offers no neat moral cure; it leaves its travellers in a hard-won willingness to remain alive, questioning, and connected in the face of despair.

The show’s central themes are love under pressure, the vulnerability of bodies and families, and the refusal of fixed moral or social roles. It finds affirmation not in certainty or purity, but in doubt, unruliness, desire, and the decision to keep reaching for others despite everything.

show: Europavisjonar, the Norwegian political satire musical by Simen Formo Hay, Johan Hveem Maurud and Oda Radoor, premiered 2025 at Det Norske Teatret
synopsis:
A commentator launches a glittering contest in which Europe’s leaders step into the spotlight as Eurovision-style contestants, each determined to sell the audience a vision of the continent’s future. Beginning with the fall of the Berlin Wall, the competition turns recent European history into a parade of campaign songs, choreography, flags, costumes and rival bids for popular approval. Boris Jeltsin sings out the exhilaration and uncertainty of a newly opened East; Tony Blair offers the confident promise of 1990s market liberalism; NATO, EU and their competing ideals of security, expansion, bureaucracy and prosperity vie for the room’s applause. Angela Merkel, Jens Stoltenberg, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Marine Le Pen, Boris Johnson, Vladimir Putin and others enter the arena not as distant figures in a textbook but as performers with microphones, political slogans and increasingly incompatible dreams.

At first, the contest races forward with the exuberance of a televised final. Each number reframes a decisive moment—glasnost, economic growth, consumerism, the financial crisis and the refugee crisis—as a chance to win points. The audience is invited to judge: should Europe choose growth and shopping, military rearmament and balance of power, or the cumbersome machinery of the EU? Beneath the competition’s sparkle, however, the succession of “visions” starts to expose the costs of the choices on offer.

As the timeline reaches the present, the show’s playful contest grows harder to sustain. The war surrounding Ukraina and Russland breaks the premise open, while the conflict between Israel and Palestina further strains the fantasy that disagreement can be neatly resolved by a vote. Song, spectacle and comedy continue, but grief, division and fear press through the glitter as the contestants and audience confront what their visions have produced.

The musical turns democracy into both a dazzling public ritual and a fragile act of collective judgment. Its central concern is whether people can still live together amid war, nationalism, polarisation and competing claims to power—and whether shared ideals can survive when the show of unity breaks down.

show: Änglagård - The Musical, the Swedish musical after Colin Nutley's 1992 film, premiered at Oscarsteatern in Stockholm
synopsis:
Rut Flogfält opens a letter addressed to her husband, Axel Flogfält, and learns the secret that will poison her life for twenty years: Axel is the father of five-year-old Fanny, born to Alice, who has already left Yxared for Berlin. Rut says nothing. She keeps the letter, buries the truth, and resolves to carry it with her to the grave.

Two decades later, Erik Zander dies, apparently without an heir. Axel sees his chance to acquire Änglagård, the grand estate he covets, but his plans collapse when Fanny Zander arrives from Berlin with Zac Paulin, her flamboyant, worldly friend. Fanny has only just learned that Erik was her grandfather. Claiming Änglagård as her inheritance, she settles into the house and begins searching for the identity of the father she has never known.

Their arrival jolts Yxared out of its complacency. Fanny and Zac’s style, freedom, and refusal to conform provoke gossip and hostility among villagers who defend tradition and respectability. Yet they also find unexpected allies: Mårten Flogfält, Axel and Rut’s son; the elderly brothers Gottfrid Pettersson and Ivar Pettersson; and Henning Collmer, the local pastor. As friendships form and old loyalties shift, Axel confronts the consequences of a past he did not know had been concealed from him, while Rut is forced to face the damage caused by her silence. Fanny’s determination to uncover her origins drives the hidden family connection toward exposure, changing the relationships within the Flogfält household and the community around Änglagård.

The musical centres on belonging, inheritance, and the cost of secrets kept in the name of respectability. It sets prejudice and rigid tradition against self-definition, chosen friendship, and the possibility of reconciliation.

show: Pippi på sirkus, the Swedish circus musical with music by Björn Ulvaeus, after Astrid Lindgren's Pippi Longstocking
synopsis:
Pippi, Tommy and Annika step into the glittering manesjen for Pippi’s first visit to the circus, where nothing seems as marvellous to her as the possibility of joining in. While the audience is expected to sit quietly and admire the acts, Pippi watches the performers with growing impatience. Miss Carmencita, the circus princess, dazzles the ring; Elvira balances high above it; and the circus’s feats of nerve, strength and spectacle unfold under the commands of the irritable Sirkusdirektøren. But Pippi has little interest in obeying the usual rules of a performance. She leaps into the action, turning acts meant to impress her into challenges she feels compelled to answer herself.

Her fearless interruptions create one misunderstanding after another. Pippi matches the circus artists in daring, makes the carefully managed programme increasingly unpredictable, and wins over the crowd precisely because she refuses to remain a passive spectator. Tommy and Annika are swept along by the commotion as the Sirkusdirektøren struggles to retain control of a show that Pippi keeps remaking in her own exuberant image.

The contest reaches its peak when the audience is invited to face Sterke Adolf, billed as the world’s strongest man. Pippi accepts without hesitation. What begins as the circus’s great demonstration of masculine strength becomes her triumph: she proves herself stronger than Sterke Adolf and leaves the established order of the manesjen thoroughly overturned. The show closes with Pippi’s irrepressible spirit prevailing over greed, rules and intimidation.

The musical celebrates curiosity, play and the freedom to refuse a role imposed by adults or institutions. It also turns Pippi’s strength into a challenge to vanity, greed and the idea that anyone must stay on the sidelines.

show: Emil i Lönneberga, the Swedish family musical after Astrid Lindgren's stories, staged at Intiman in Stockholm
synopsis:
Emil races through the yard at Katthult with another bright idea already gathering speed, while his family braces for the consequences. He means no harm, yet every innocent impulse seems to turn into a spectacular hyss: a soppskål becomes stuck over his head, and his little sister Ida ends up being raised high in the flaggstången because Emil believes she wants to see all the way to Mariannelund. When the grown-ups become furious, Emil is sent to the snickerboa, where punishment turns into solitude, carving, and time to dream up whatever comes next.

Around him, life on the farm carries on with warmth, work, songs, meals, arguments, and affection. Emil’s parents try to preserve order; Ida is torn between admiration and alarm; Lina reacts to every upheaval with outrage; and Alfred, Emil’s trusted friend, sees the kindness beneath the chaos. Even Lukas, Emil’s faithful horse, is part of the boy’s adventures. The ordinary routines of Katthult are repeatedly interrupted by Emil’s schemes, but his mischief is never simply selfish. His imagination exposes the stiff rules of the adults’ world, and the trouble he causes often grows from his wish to help, discover, or make life more exciting.

As Emil confronts the results of his actions, the people around him begin to recognise that the boy’s wild energy also contains courage and a generous heart. What first looks like disobedience becomes a series of lessons in responsibility, forgiveness, and seeing others more clearly.

At its heart, the musical celebrates childhood imagination and the way love can survive noise, mistakes, and exasperation. It also suggests that kindness and bravery may appear in the most unruly child in the room.

show: Ronja Rövardotter, the Swedish family musical with music by Björn Isfält, after Astrid Lindgren's novel
synopsis:
Ronja is born in Mattisborgen on a night of thunder, when a lightning strike tears the fortress in two and opens the chasm called Helvetesgapet. She grows up cherished by her father, Mattis, watched over by Lovis, and surrounded by Mattis’s boisterous rövare. When she is old enough to leave the safety of the castle, Ronja ventures into Mattisskogen, where grådvärgar, vildvittror and rumpnissar make every path unpredictable. On the edge of Helvetesgapet she encounters Birk, the son of Mattis’s sworn rival, Borka, whose band has occupied the other half of Mattisborgen. Their first meetings are combative, each defending the honour of a parent’s name, but daring tests, narrow escapes and shared discoveries turn hostility into a secret friendship.

Mattis and Borka deepen their feud as each tries to dominate the forest and outwit the other. Caught between their fathers’ pride, Ronja and Birk refuse to inherit the hatred. When Mattis captures Birk, Ronja gives herself to Borka in exchange for her friend’s freedom. Mattis feels betrayed and, in anger, rejects her as his daughter. Birk and Ronja leave both robber bands behind and make a home in Björngrottan, facing hunger, cold and the dangers of the forest together while proving that they can survive without the adults’ quarrel.

Their absence forces Mattis and Borka to confront what their rivalry has cost them. As Ronja and Birk hold firm to their loyalty, the feud loses its power. Reconciliation becomes possible only when the fathers accept responsibility, let go of wounded pride and recognise the courage of the children they tried to control.

The show centres on friendship that crosses inherited boundaries, and on the courage to choose conscience over family loyalty. It also treats growing up as a process of claiming independence while leaving open the possibility of forgiveness, peace and renewed family bonds.

show: Så som i himmelen, the Swedish musical created by Kay Pollak, Carin Pollak and Fredrik Kempe, after the 2004 Swedish film
synopsis:
Daniel Daréus collapses at the height of an international conducting career, his failing heart forcing him to abandon the relentless life that has consumed him. Seeking silence, he returns to the Norrland village where, as a bullied child, he learned to protect himself from other people. He buys the old schoolhouse and hopes to remain anonymous, but the local kyrkokör soon draws him in. At first he agrees only to listen; then, almost against his will, he begins to lead them.

Daniel refuses to train the singers into polished performers. Instead, he asks them to listen for their own voices and for the sound they can make together. The work unsettles the village’s routines and exposes long-buried wounds. Lena, warm, impulsive and restless for a larger life, becomes Daniel’s closest companion and eventually his lover. Gabriella, trapped in a violent marriage to Conny, discovers an extraordinary voice and gradually finds the courage to resist him. Tore, long treated as an outsider, is welcomed into the choir. Holmfrid finally confronts Arne’s cruel jokes, while Arne must learn that ambition and control can wound the very people he claims to support.

The changes also threaten Stig, the kyrkoherde, whose authority and rigid faith are challenged by Daniel’s unconventional methods; Inger, weary of her unhappy marriage, begins to claim a life of her own. As the choir prepares to sing beyond the village, its members become braver, more honest, and more connected. Daniel, however, cannot escape the fragility of his health. In the climactic performance, surrounded by the voices he has helped release, he experiences the communal music he has always sought before his heart finally gives out.

The show’s central themes are the search for one’s authentic voice, the healing force of music, and the courage to break free from fear, shame and oppression. It also contrasts authority and isolation with love, vulnerability and the transforming power of community.

show: The Julekalender, the Danish Christmas musical by the comedy group De Nattergale, after their 1991 Danish TV series
synopsis:
A storm-tossed craft carries Frits, Hansi, and Günther to an old nissehule in Jylland, close to the home of the potato-growing couple Oluf and Gertrud Sand. They have been sent to recover the key to a spilledåse whose music keeps the elderly nisse Gammel Nok alive. Their mission is urgent: the key was left behind when the nisser fled long ago, and without it Gammel Nok’s life melody will run down. The three travellers bring Den Store Bog, a precious volume that can supply answers to almost anything, but which must never be captured by a Nåsåer.

Their landing goes badly, leaving their means of escape damaged and forcing them to remain in the cave while they search for the key. Nearby, everyday Christmas preparations unfold in the Sand household, where Gertrud’s extensive box of decorations and “æ mistelten” become part of the domestic commotion. Into this familiar setting comes Benny, a travelling salesman from Copenhagen who knocks at Oluf and Gertrud’s door, claiming his car has broken down and asking to stay the night. His cheerful human guise conceals a far more dangerous purpose: he is a Nåsåer, one of the enemies from whom the nisser once escaped.

Benny’s arrival turns the quest into a contest of concealment, mistaken encounters, and mounting danger. While Frits, Hansi, and Günther try to locate the life-saving key and protect Den Store Bog, Benny manoeuvres around the Sands’ home in pursuit of the book and the power it contains. The two worlds—the nisser’ secret cave and Oluf and Gertrud’s ordinary Christmas household—draw ever closer, putting Gammel Nok’s survival and the nisser’ safety at stake.

At heart, the show turns a Christmas rescue mission into a comic clash between fellowship and greed, secrecy and intrusion. It celebrates the persistence of tradition and communal warmth while placing them under pressure from a threatening outsider.

show: Ternet Ninja Live, the new Danish musical after Anders Matthesen's Ternet Ninja, adapted by Clemens Telling and directed by Sargun Oshana
synopsis:
Uncle Stewart arrives at Aske’s birthday carrying an unusual present: a ninja teddy bear from Thailand, sewn from striking checkered cloth. The gift gives Aske something to cling to at a time when nearly everything else in his life feels wrong. At home, his mother’s attention is consumed by her new partner, Jørn, and Jørn’s irritating son, Sune; at school, Jessica from 8th grade barely notices him; and in the playground, Glenn and his gang make sure he never forgets his place in the pecking order. Late that night, after the birthday has ended and Aske has gone to bed, the toy reveals that it is alive. The ternede ninja can talk, move, fight—and has little patience for politeness or restraint.

Aske soon realizes that this is no ordinary sidekick. Beneath its soft exterior, the ninja is dangerously capable, sharp-tongued, and driven by an uncompromising need for justice and revenge. Its arrival gives Aske a possible weapon against the humiliations that surround him: the bullies, his unreturned crush on Jessica, and the disorder of his blended family. Yet the same force that promises to defend him also threatens to turn every grievance into a battle. Aske must navigate the chaotic influence of the ninja while dealing with Stewart Stardust, Mie and Fie, Arne Nougatgren, Philip Eberfrø, and the other larger-than-life people in his world. What begins as a birthday surprise becomes an escalating adventure in which a lonely boy’s wish for help collides with a protector whose idea of solving problems can be lethal.

The show brings together outsiderhood, family upheaval, schoolyard cruelty, first love, and the seductive appeal of instant revenge. At its heart, it asks how far justice can go before it becomes violence—and whether Aske can find courage without becoming ruled by anger.

show: De Spiekpietjes Musical - Paniek in de Speelgoedfabriek, the Flemish (Belgian) children's musical written by Tom Dewulf and Thais Vanderheyden, staged at Trixxo Theater in Hasselt
synopsis:
Inside Sint’s speelgoedfabriek the usual orderly flow of toys, packages and sweets is about to be thrown off course: the brave-kindjes-meter is racing wildly upward. Each well-behaved child makes the meter rise, triggering the factory to produce still more presents and candy; this year, there are so many flinke kindjes that the machinery can no longer keep pace. Its alarms begin to tremble and beep, and a speelgoedramp looms: unless the meter is calmed, the speelgoedfabriek could explode.

It is the Spiekpietjes who walk straight into it. The small Sinterklaashulpjes are taken on their first tour through the speelgoed- en snoepfabriek, but their exciting visit becomes an emergency mission when they see the scale of the runaway production. With the factory overwhelmed and time running out, they must work together to find a way to lower the frantic meter before its demands bury the workshop in an impossible mountain of toys and treats.

Their solution turns the problem on its head. Since the meter responds to children being flink and braaf, the Spiekpietjes try to make it settle by filling the moment with deliberately naughty-sounding fun: vieze woorden and vuile moppen. The children are invited to help, joining the Spiekpietjes in the effort to bring the unstable machine back under control. Through collective playfulness, the crisis is transformed from a frightening disaster into a lively rescue inside Sint’s extraordinary factory.

The show centres on cooperation, imaginative problem-solving and the joy of taking part rather than watching from the sidelines. It also playfully suggests that being good need not mean being solemn: laughter, mischief and shared fun can help solve a crisis.
